text.en: Rita and Shabnam went to the market to buy fruits and vegetables. The vegetable seller was weighing the vegetables on a scale. Half a pumpkin sat on one side and metal weights sat on the other. Rita asked how much the half pumpkin would weigh, and Shabnam wondered how many bananas make one kilogram. In this chapter you will learn to guess weights, check them with a balance, and measure how much water or milk a bottle can hold.

In Class 3 you learnt about weight and capacity, and you remember the 1 kilogram salt packet and the 1 litre bottle. Some things are heavy and some are light, and we can put animals or objects in order from the heaviest to the lightest. An elephant is much heavier than a cat, and a cat is much heavier than a leaf. You can often tell which thing is heavy because it needs more effort to lift, like your school bag with all your books in it.
Before we weigh something, we can estimate, which means making a sensible guess. At the market, ask yourself whether six bananas weigh less than one kilogram or more than one kilogram, and tick your guess. Then use a weighing balance to check, and find out how close your guess was. Estimating again and again makes your guesses better and better.
We measure weight in kilograms and in grams, and we often write kg for kilogram and g for gram. A kilogram is a large unit and a gram is a small unit. 1 kilogram is the same as 1000 grams. Two packets of 500 grams make 1000 grams, which is 1 kilogram, so one packet of 500 grams is half a kilogram. Four packets of 250 grams make 1 kilogram, so one packet of 250 grams is a quarter of a kilogram. Ten packets of 100 grams also make 1 kilogram.
A pan balance tilts towards the heavier side, and it stays level when both pans hold the same weight. If a 500 gram packet of dal sits on the left pan, two 250 gram packets on the right pan will balance it, so 250 g is half of 500 g. Look at the picture on the board, where one 500 g packet and two 250 g packets balance each other. Draw an arrow on the side that goes down, and you will know where the heavier weight is.
We use kilograms for heavy things like rice, atta, sugar, a school bag or a person. We use grams for light things like a pen, a leaf, a pinch of haldi or a bar of soap. If the same object is ten grams per eraser, then five erasers weigh the same as a 50 gram haldi packet, ten erasers weigh the same as a 100 gram soap bar, and twenty-five erasers weigh as much as 250 grams of sugar.
Mr Shrinathan has to pack 1 kg of Kaju-katli in boxes of different sizes. In 500 gram boxes he needs 2 boxes, because 500 plus 500 is 1000 grams. In 250 gram boxes he needs 4 boxes, and in 100 gram boxes he needs 10 boxes. In 50 gram boxes he needs 20 boxes, because it takes twenty boxes of 50 grams to make 1000 grams. So the smaller the box, the more boxes we need for the same total weight.
There are different weighing machines, like the pan balance, the spring scale and the machine at a shop, and each one suits a different job. Ask at home how much atta, rice, pulses and sugar your family uses in a month, and write the weight in kilograms. When you lift a packet of flour or rice you feel its weight in your arms, so try lifting things and say which ones you can lift easily and which need a lot of effort. Ten 1 kg packets make 10 kg, twenty make 20 kg, and fifty make 50 kg. Mirabai Chanu, an Indian weightlifter, won the silver medal in the women’s 49 kg event at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, and she lifted a total of 202 kg.
Capacity tells us how much a container can hold, for example how much water your bottle holds. We measure capacity in litres and millilitres, and we often write l for litre and ml for millilitre. 1 litre is the same as 1000 millilitres. Two bottles of 500 ml fill one litre, so 500 ml is half a litre. Four bottles of 250 ml fill one litre, so 250 ml is a quarter of a litre. Ten bottles of 100 ml also fill one litre. Look at the picture on the board to see four 250 ml bottles becoming one litre.
Dosing cups, droppers and teaspoons measure very small amounts. It takes ten cups of 10 ml to fill a 100 ml bottle, twenty-five to fill a 250 ml glass, fifty to fill a 500 ml vessel and a hundred to fill a 1 litre bottle. A dropper holds about 1 ml, so ten droppers fill a 10 ml dosing cup. Eye drops use less than 1 ml at a time, while cooking oil and cough syrup use different amounts, and you can find out each by asking at home.
Mr Krishna packs perfumed oil in bottles of different sizes, and each customer wants 1 litre in total. With 500 ml bottles a customer gets 2 bottles, and with 200 ml bottles the customer gets 5 bottles. With 100 ml bottles the customer gets 10 bottles, and with 50 ml bottles the customer gets 20 bottles. To check any answer, multiply the number of bottles by the size of each bottle and see if you get 1000 ml.
A person should drink a certain amount of water every day, and you can find out how many glasses or bottles you drink. A crow drinks only a few spoonfuls at a time, but an elephant drinks a very large amount of water every day. Taking a shower, washing clothes, watering plants and watering a field all use different amounts of water, and you can compare which job uses the most. Put a container under a slowly dripping tap for an hour and see how much water is wasted, then think how much would be lost in a day or a week. Saving water at home, like closing the tap properly, helps everyone.

problem.en: How many 250 g packets balance one 500 g packet of dal?

text.en: Put the 500 g packet on the left pan.

why.en: The right pan must hold the same weight to balance it.

text.en: Put 250 g packets on the right pan one by one.
One packet gives 250 g and two packets give 500 g.
So 2 packets of 250 g balance 500 g, and 250 g is half of 500 g.

why.en: The pans are level when the weights are equal.

problem.en: A customer wants 1 litre of oil in bottles of 200 ml. How many bottles will she get?

text.en: 1 litre is 1000 ml.
We reached 1000 ml after counting five bottles.
So she gets 5 bottles.

why.en: The total of the bottles equals 1 litre.

problem.en: Mr Shrinathan packs 1 kg of Kaju-katli in boxes of 50 g. How many boxes does he need?

text.en: 1 kg is 1000 g.
Ten boxes of 50 g hold 500 g.
Another ten boxes hold the other 500 g.
So he needs 20 boxes of 50 g.

problem.en: A 50 gram haldi packet weighs the same as how many 10 gram erasers?

text.en: Count in 10s until you reach 50.
10, 20, 30, 40, 50 is five counts.
So 5 erasers weigh the same as the haldi packet.

prompt.en: Explain how kilograms and grams are related, and how litres and millilitres are related, using packet and bottle examples.

requiredIdeas.en: 1 kg is 1000 g and 1 l is 1000 ml
500 g and 500 ml are half of a kg or a litre
250 g and 250 ml are a quarter of a kg or a litre
Two 500s, four 250s or ten 100s make one whole
Smaller packets or bottles mean more of them are needed

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking 250 g is half a kilogram
Thinking a bigger number of bottles means a bigger total when each bottle is smaller

points.en: 1 kilogram is the same as 1000 grams, and 1 litre is the same as 1000 millilitres.
500 g or 500 ml is half, and 250 g or 250 ml is a quarter, of a kilogram or a litre.
A pan balance tilts towards the heavier side and stays level when the weights are equal.
Use kilograms for heavy things and grams for light things.
Estimate first, then check with a balance or a measuring bottle.
Saving water, for example by fixing drips, matters in everyday life.
